questions.problem: A surface $S$ is defined by $z=f(x,y).$ The curve $C$ is the intersection of $S$ with the plane $y=\pi .$ Given that the point $P$ with $x$-coordinate $1$ lies on $C$, and that ${f}_{x}=(x+y){e}^{\operatorname{cos}⁡(xy)}$, find the slope of the tangent to $C$ at $P.$
questions.worked_solution:
The curve $C$ is the intersection of the surface $z=f(x,y)$ with the plane $y=\pi .$ Hence, the slope of the tangent to the curve $C$ at the point where $x=1$ will be given by the partial derivative ${f}_{x}(1,\pi ).$ 

To get the slope, we evaluate the partial derivative ${f}_{x}(x,y)$ at $(1,\pi ):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{x}(1,\pi ) & =(1+\pi ){e}^{\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi \cdot 1)} \\  & =(1+\pi ){e}^{-1} \\  & =\frac{1+\pi }{e}\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: The curve $C$ is the intersection of a surface $S,$ defined by $z=f(x,y),$ with the plane $y=2.$ Given that the point $P(-\frac{\pi }{2},2,2\pi )$ lies on $C$, and that ${f}_{x}=\operatorname{sin}⁡x+\frac{xy}{\pi }$, find the equations of the tangent line to $C$ at $P.$
questions.worked_solution:
The curve $C$ is the intersection of the surface $z=f(x,y)$ with the plane $y=2.$ Hence, the slope of the tangent to the curve at the point $P(-\frac{\pi }{2},2,2\pi )$ will be given by the partial derivative $\frac{∂z}{∂x}{|}_{(-\pi /2,2)}.$

To get the slope, we evaluate the partial derivative $\frac{∂z}{∂x}$ at $(-\frac{\pi }{2},2):$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂z}{∂x}{|}_{(-\pi /2,2)} & =\operatorname{sin}⁡(-\frac{\pi }{2})+\frac{(-\frac{\pi }{2})(2)}{\pi } \\  & =-1-1 \\  & =-2\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we use the point-slope form of a straight line:

$$
\begin{aligned}z-z{|}_{(-\pi /2,2)} & =\frac{∂z}{∂x}{|}_{(-\pi /2,2)}(x-(-\frac{\pi }{2})) \\ z-2\pi  & =-2(x+\frac{\pi }{2}) \\ z & =-2x+\pi \end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the tangent line to the curve $C$ at $P(-\frac{\pi }{2},2,2\pi )$ can be given as the intersection of two planes, as follows:

$$
{\begin{aligned}y=2 \\ z=-2x+\pi \end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: The curve $C$ is the intersection of a surface $S,$ defined by $z=f(x,y),$ with the plane $x=1.$ Given that the point $P(1,2,4)$ lies on $C$, and that ${f}_{y}=\frac{3x+y}{\sqrt{6xy+{y}^{2}}}$, find the equations of the tangent line to $C$ at $P.$
questions.worked_solution:
The curve $C$ is the intersection of the surface $z=f(x,y)$ with the plane $x=1.$ Hence, the slope of the tangent to the curve at the point $P(1,2,4)$ will be given by the partial derivative $\frac{∂z}{∂y}{|}_{(1,2)}.$

To get the slope, we evaluate the partial derivative $\frac{∂z}{∂y}$ at $(1,2):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{y}(1,2) & =\frac{3(1)+(2)}{\sqrt{6(1)(2)+(2)^{2}}} \\  & =\frac{5}{\sqrt{16}} \\  & =\frac{5}{4}\end{aligned}
$$

 

Now, we use the point-slope form of a straight line:

$$
\begin{aligned}z-z{|}_{(1,2)} & =\frac{∂z}{∂y}{|}_{(1,2)}(y-2) \\ z-4 & =\frac{5}{4}(y-2) \\ z & =\frac{5}{4}y+\frac{3}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the tangent line to the curve $C$ at $P(1,2,4)$ can be given as the intersection of two planes, as follows:

$$
{\begin{aligned}x=1 \\ z=\frac{5}{4}y+\frac{3}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: The curve $C$ is the intersection of a surface $S,$ defined by $z=f(x,y),$ with the plane $x=\frac{\pi }{2}.$ Given that the point $P(\frac{\pi }{2},1,0)$ lies on $C$, and that ${f}_{y}=2\operatorname{sin}⁡(xy)-\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2}y)$, which of the following gives a tangent vector to $C$ at $P?$
questions.worked_solution:
The curve $C$ is the intersection of the surface with the plane $x=\frac{\pi }{2}.$ Hence, the slope of the tangent to the curve $C$ at the point $P$ will be given by the partial derivative ${f}_{y}(\frac{\pi }{2},1).$ 

To get the slope, we evaluate the partial derivative ${f}_{y}(x,y)$ at $(\frac{\pi }{2},1):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{y}(\frac{\pi }{2},1) & =2\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2}\cdot 1)-\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2}\cdot 1) \\  & =2\cdot 1-0 \\  & =2\end{aligned}
$$

 

Now, we use the point-slope form of a straight line:

$$
\begin{aligned}z-f(\frac{\pi }{2},1) & ={f}_{y}(\frac{\pi }{2},1)(y-1) \\ z-0 & =2(y-1) \\ z & =2y-2\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the tangent line to the curve $C$ at $P(\frac{\pi }{2},1,0)$ can be given as the intersection of two planes:

$$
{\begin{aligned}x=\frac{\pi }{2} \\ z=2y-2\end{aligned}
$$

Next, notice that:

- For the plane $x=\frac{\pi }{2},$ a normal vector to the plane is ${n}_{1}=⟨1,0,0⟩.$

- For the plane $z=2y-2$ (or $2y-z-2=0$), a normal vector to the plane is ${n}_{2}=⟨0,2,-1⟩.$

Finally, to find a direction vector for the tangent line, we calculate the cross product of these normal vectors:

$$
\begin{aligned}{n}_{1}\times {n}_{2} & =⟨1,0,0⟩\times ⟨0,2,-1⟩ \\  & =\left|\begin{aligned}i & j & k \\ 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 2 & -1\end{aligned}\right| \\  & =j+2\,k \\  & =⟨0,1,2⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, a tangent vector to $C$ at $P$ is $⟨0,1,2⟩.$

questions.problem: The curve $C$ is the intersection of a surface $S,$ defined by $z=f(x,y),$ with the plane $x=1.$ Given that the point $P(1,0,-1)$ lies on $C$, and that ${f}_{y}=x{e}^{xy}-2\operatorname{cos}⁡y$, which of the following gives a tangent vector to $C$ at $P?$
questions.worked_solution:
The curve $C$ is the intersection of the surface with the plane $x=1.$ Hence, the slope of the tangent to the curve $C$ at the point $P$ will be given by the partial derivative ${f}_{y}(1,0).$ 

To get the slope, we evaluate the partial derivative ${f}_{y}(x,y)$ at $(1,0):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{y}(1,0) & =1\cdot {e}^{1\cdot 0}-2\operatorname{cos}⁡0 \\  & =1\cdot 1-2\cdot 1 \\  & =-1\end{aligned}
$$

 

Now, we use the point-slope form of a straight line:

$$
\begin{aligned}z-f(1,0) & ={f}_{y}(1,0)(y-0) \\ z-(-1) & =(-1)y \\ z & =-y-1\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the tangent line to the curve $C$ at $P(1,0,-1)$ can be given as the intersection of two planes:

$$
{\begin{aligned}x=1 \\ z=-y-1\end{aligned}
$$

Next, notice that:

- For the plane $x=1,$ a normal vector to the plane is ${n}_{1}=⟨1,0,0⟩.$

- For the plane $z=-y-1$ (or $y+z+1=0$), a normal vector to the plane is ${n}_{2}=⟨0,1,1⟩.$

Finally, to find a direction vector for the tangent line, we calculate the cross product of these normal vectors:

$$
\begin{aligned}{n}_{1}\times {n}_{2} & =⟨1,0,0⟩\times ⟨0,1,1⟩ \\  & =\left|\begin{aligned}i & j & k \\ 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 1\end{aligned}\right| \\  & =-j+k\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, a tangent vector to $C$ at $P$ is $-j+k.$

The curve $C$ is the intersection of the surface with the plane $x=-\frac{\pi }{2}.$ Hence, the slope of the tangent to the curve $C$ at the point $P$ will be given by the partial derivative ${f}_{y}(-\frac{\pi }{2},0).$

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{y}(-\frac{\pi }{2},0) & =\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡(-\frac{\pi }{2})\operatorname{cos}⁡0}{2} \\  & =\frac{(-1)\cdot 1}{2} \\  & =-\frac{1}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

 

Now, we use the point-slope form of a straight line:

$$
\begin{aligned}z-f(-\frac{\pi }{2},0) & ={f}_{y}(-\frac{\pi }{2},0)(y-0) \\ z-2 & =-\frac{1}{2}y \\ z & =-\frac{1}{2}y+2\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the tangent line to the curve $C$ at $P(-\frac{\pi }{2},0,2)$ can be given as the intersection of two planes:

$$
{\begin{aligned}x=-\frac{\pi }{2} \\ z=-\frac{1}{2}y+2\end{aligned}
$$

Next, notice that:

- For the plane $x=-\frac{\pi }{2},$ a normal vector to the plane is ${n}_{1}=⟨1,0,0⟩.$

- For the plane $z=-\frac{1}{2}y+2$ (or $y+2z-4=0$), a normal vector to the plane is ${n}_{2}=⟨0,1,2⟩.$

$$

$$

questions.problem: The curve $C$ is the intersection of a surface $S,$ defined by $z=f(x,y),$ with the plane $y=1.$ Given that the point $P(-1,1,-1)$ lies on $C$, and that ${f}_{x}=3{e}^{x+y}-\operatorname{ln}⁡|xy|$, which of the following gives a tangent vector to $C$ at $P?$
questions.worked_solution:
The curve $C$ is the intersection of the surface with the plane $y=1.$ Hence, the slope of the tangent to the curve $C$ at the point $P$ will be given by the partial derivative ${f}_{x}(-1,1).$ 

To get the slope, we evaluate the partial derivative ${f}_{x}(x,y)$ at $(-1,1):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{x}(-1,1) & =3{e}^{-1+1}-\operatorname{ln}⁡|(-1)\cdot 1| \\  & =3\cdot 1-\operatorname{ln}⁡1 \\  & =3-0 \\  & =3\end{aligned}
$$

 

Now, we use the point-slope form of a straight line:

$$
\begin{aligned}z-f(-1,1) & ={f}_{x}(-1,1)(x-(-1)) \\ z-(-1) & =3(x+1) \\ z+1 & =3x+3 \\ z & =3x+2\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the tangent line to the curve $C$ at $P(-1,1,-1)$ can be given as the intersection of two planes:

$$
{\begin{aligned}y=1 \\ z=3x+2\end{aligned}
$$

Next, notice that:

- For the plane $y=1,$ a normal vector to the plane is ${n}_{1}=⟨0,1,0⟩.$

- For the plane $z=3x+2$ (or $3x-z+2=0$), a normal vector to the plane is ${n}_{2}=⟨3,0,-1⟩.$

Finally, to find a direction vector for the tangent line, we calculate the cross product of these normal vectors:

$$
\begin{aligned}{n}_{1}\times {n}_{2} & =⟨0,1,0⟩\times ⟨3,0,-1⟩ \\  & =\left|\begin{aligned}i & j & k \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 3 & 0 & -1\end{aligned}\right| \\  & =-i-3\,k \\  & =⟨-1,0,-3⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, since $⟨-1,0,-3⟩$ is parallel to the tangent line, then $-⟨-1,0,-3⟩=⟨1,0,3⟩$ is also parallel to it.

canonical_examples.problem: The curve $C$ is the intersection of a surface $S,$ defined by $z=f(x,y),$ with the plane $y=\pi.$ Given that the point $P(1,\pi,-1)$ lies on $C,$ and that $f_x = y\cos(xy) + \cos y,$ find the equations of the tangent line to $C$ at $P.$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
The curve $C$ is the intersection of the surface $z = f(x,y)$ with the plane $y=\pi.$ So, the slope of the tangent to the curve at the point $P(1,\pi,-1)$ will be given by the partial derivative $\dfrac {\partial z} {\partial x} \Bigg|_{(1,\pi)}.$ 

To get the slope, we evaluate the partial derivative $\dfrac {\partial z} {\partial x}$ at $(1,\pi)\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂z}{∂x}{|}_{(1,\pi )} & =\pi \operatorname{cos}⁡(1\cdot \pi )+\operatorname{cos}⁡\pi  \\  & =\pi (-1)+(-1) \\  & =-\pi -1\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we use the point-slope form of a straight line:

$$
\begin{aligned}z-z{|}_{(1,\pi )} & =\frac{∂z}{∂x}{|}_{(1,\pi )}(x-1) \\ z-(-1) & =(-\pi -1)(x-1) \\ z+1 & =(-\pi -1)x+\pi +1 \\ z & =-(\pi +1)x+\pi \end{aligned}
$$

The equation above represents a line in the $xz$-plane. The $xz$-plane through the point $P(1,\pi,-1)$ has the equation $y=\pi.$

So, the tangent line to the curve $C$ at $P(1,\pi,-1)$ is given by the intersection of the following planes:

$$
{\begin{aligned}y=\pi  \\ z=-(\pi +1)x+\pi \end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Finding the Tangent Vector to a Curve at a Point
canonical_examples.problem: The curve $C$ is the intersection of a surface $S,$ defined by $z=f(x,y),$ with the plane $y=1.$ Given that the point $P(0,1,1)$ lies on $C,$ and that $f_x =  \dfrac{\sqrt{2} \pi}{4} \sin{\left(2 x + \dfrac{\pi y}{4} \right)},$ find a tangent vector to $C$ at $P.$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
The curve $C$ is the intersection of the surface with the plane $y=1.$ So, the slope of the tangent to the curve $C$ at the point $P$ will be given by the partial derivative $f_x(0,1).$ 

To get the slope, we evaluate the partial derivative $f_x(x,y)$ at $(0,1)\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{x}(0,1) & =\frac{\sqrt{2}\pi }{4}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2(0)+\frac{\pi (1)}{4}) \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{2}\pi }{4}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{4}) \\  & =\frac{\pi }{4}\end{aligned}
$$

 

Now, we use the point-slope form of a straight line:

$$
\begin{aligned}z-f(0,1) & ={f}_{x}(0,1)(x-0) \\ z-1 & =\frac{\pi }{4}x \\ z & =\frac{\pi }{4}x+1\end{aligned}
$$

The equation above represents a line in the $xz$-plane. The $xz$-plane through the point $P(0,1,1)$ has the equation $y=1.$

So, the tangent line to the curve $C$ at $P(0,1,1)$ is given by the intersection of the following planes:

$$
{\begin{aligned}y=1 \\ z=\frac{\pi }{4}x+1\end{aligned}
$$

To find a tangent vector, we can find a normal vector to each plane and compute their cross product.

- For the plane $y = 1,$ we write $0x + 1y + 0z = 1$ and find the normal vector $\mathbf{n}_1 = \langle 0,1,0 \rangle.$

- For the plane $z = \dfrac{\pi}{4} x +1,$ we write $-\dfrac{\pi}{4} x + 0y + 1z = 1$ and find the normal vector $\mathbf{n}_2 = \left\langle -\dfrac{\pi}4,0,1 \right\rangle.$

Computing the cross product, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{n}_{1}\times {n}_{2} & =⟨0,1,0⟩\times ⟨-\frac{\pi }{4},0,1⟩ \\  & =\left|\begin{aligned}i & j & k \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ -\pi /4 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}\right| \\  & =i+\frac{\pi }{4}\,k.\end{aligned}
$$

At this point, we've found a tangent vector, and this could be our final answer. However, just to make our answer a little nicer, we can multiply the vector by $4$ to yield a simpler, parallel vector:

$$
\begin{aligned}4\cdot (i+\frac{\pi }{4}\,k)=4\,i+\pi \,k\end{aligned}
$$
